# HFT Onsite Round 3 — Sort Complexity + Linux Fundamentals + tail(n) Design

[← Citadel](../README.md) · [Every Citadel question](../../citadel.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/citadel-hft-onsite-fundamentals)

`complexity-analysis` `cs-fundamentals` `io` `operating-systems` `sorting`

---

## Requirements

This is an entirely verbal, whiteboard-style round with no live coding submission. The interviewer leads, and the candidate answers. Reported areas of coverage:

- Explain the conventional sorting algorithms along with their time and space complexity. Quicksort receives the greatest focus: average versus worst-case behavior, methods for choosing pivots, and situations in which quicksort beats or falls behind heapsort and mergesort.
- Linux basics: shared memory (`shm`, `mmap`), interrupt processing, context switches, and system calls.
- Design: output the final `n` lines from an extremely large file. Cover possible optimizations, including seeking backward, reading in chunks, using `mmap`, and handling a case where `n` is also large.

## Notes

- Quicksort runs in average-case `O(n log n)` time and can reach `O(n^2)` on adversarial data, including sorted or reverse-sorted input with a naive pivot and all-identical values with two-way partitioning. Possible safeguards include a randomized pivot, median-of-three selection, and introspective sorting that changes to heapsort once recursion depth passes `2 log n`; three-way partitioning is useful when duplicates dominate. State all three.
- Shared memory can be established with `shm_open` and `mmap` under POSIX, or with `shmget` and `shmat` under System V. It supports low-latency communication between processes and is combined with semaphores or futexes for synchronization. It matters in HFT because it avoids copying data between producer and consumer processes running on the same host.
- Interrupts may be hardware- or software-generated, and handlers commonly use a top-half / bottom-half arrangement: the interrupt service routine acknowledges the event and postpones expensive work to a tasklet or softirq. NIC interrupt coalescing spreads the per-packet expense across batches. In HFT, reducing interrupt delay through user-space NIC busy-polling with DPDK or another kernel-bypass approach is a recognized design pattern.
- Running `tail -n` against a massive file uses the same reverse-seeking approach as the [reverse-file-tac-implementation](#) problem: call `seekg(0, std::ios::end)`, move backward through fixed-size chunks while counting `\n` characters until `n` newlines have been found, and then write forward from that position. An `mmap` version exchanges virtual-memory usage for simpler index calculations. If `n` has no bound, the task becomes streaming the entire file in reverse, which the backward-chunk method handles directly.
- The Russian interviewer was reportedly conducting an intense cross-examination, with interrupted follow-ups and demands for quick responses; this is a recognized signal pattern for senior Citsec HFT positions. Regard it as part of the calibration rather than as something personal.

## Preparation

- Create a single-page reference containing every standard sort, its average- and worst-case time, space requirements, and stability. Memorize it. The opening five minutes of an HFT systems interview can vanish into this material without producing much signal, so move through it quickly.
- Read through `man shmget`, `man mmap`, and `man epoll` once. The HFT loop presumes comfort with Linux at the system-call level.
- Practice the backward file-reading technique in C++ until the `seekg / read / scan-for-newline` cycle is automatic. It comes up again in both `tac` and `tail -n` versions of the problem.
- Review an overview of kernel bypass or DPDK; one or two blog posts should suffice, allowing you to mention “user-space NIC polling to bypass the interrupt cost” when the discussion reaches that point. This interviewer was evidently testing depth in systems rather than requesting an actual driver implementation.
